segments.text: The party, the party in French is la fête. Like we have in English school fate, no, a school party in English is a school fate.
So that's interesting, we took the French word for party, fête, and we used it in English just to describe one particular type of party.
And it's not spelt like English, the French, the French is spelt f-e-t-e, and the first e has a little hat on it.
It has an accent mark over it, it looks like a triangle without the bottom, like a little hat, and that gives us fête, la fête.
Fête. How would you say you must organize the party? You must organize the party.
Dieu doit. Think about one bit at a time.
Dieu doit organiser la fête. Very good. Dieu doit organiser la fête. Good. I have to organize it. I must organize it.
Dieu doit la organiser. Good, and what happens to la? You use la, no, because you were thinking about the party, organizing the party, which is great.
But what happens to la and to organiser when they come together? Dieu doit l'organiser. So we get l'apostrophe organiser. We lose the a of la. Dieu doit l'organiser.
So talking about the party, la fête, we use la for it. But what if you were talking about something more general, like getting it done, I have to organize it, like getting it done.
What do you use for this general it? Le. So yes, we would use le, the masculine. So how would you say that? I have to organize it, like getting it done, or something general. Dieu doit l'organiser.

Good. Sounds the same, no? Because of course the le and organiser blend together. Je dois l'organiser. Very good. So le and la, they both mean it. And apart from this, le and la also mean him and her.
So now we can communicate many more ideas in French. How would you say provocation? Provocation. Take it syllable by syllable.
Provocation. Provocation. Good. And how would we get to provoke? We start with provocation. What do we do next? I finish the word in E-R.

Yes, but before you do that, what do you do? We lose the asio. We have to get rid of that. So do that and slowly. Provocare. Do it slowly. Ah, yes. Provoque. Provoque. Provoque. Good. To provoke. So how might you say you want to provoke him? We said the word for it is the same as the word for him. You want to provoke him.

Tu veux le provoque. Very good. Tu veux le provoque. The word for just. If you want to say something like you, you just want to provoke him, no? Is just. J-U-S-T-E. So spelled just like the English but with an E on the end to let us know to pronounce that final consonant. Just.

So you just want to provoke him. In French we will say you want just. The just will come there. You want just. So how would that be? You just want to provoke him. Tu veux juste le provoque. Very good. Tu veux juste le provoque. Very good. You just want to provoke him.

So again we can look at the verb like provoque and we can identify two parts. We can identify vocare which is like related to vocal and then we have pro the little bit that we're adding on to the beginning to provoke.

And this pro we can find around now like in provide, profess, promote. So we can identify now how provoque is built of two parts of that pro beginning and then that vocare base. And if we feel like it when we notice that we can experiment with it and play around and see what other words we might find in French from this vocare.

So for example, to invoke, how might that be? To invoke. Invoquer. Good. But here the I in gives us un. Invoquer. We could have revoke. To revoke like to take away, to take something away from somebody. How might that be in French? Revoke. Revoke. Good. Revoke. Good. So we didn't even need to go back to Asian words now to find revoke.

No, we could just do that switching between provoque, provoke and invoke, revoke just by noticing how provoke was built. So it's just about getting in the habit of thinking curiously and bringing all this French we already have in our English closer to the surface through this habit of curiosity.

To see in French is voir. Voir. Voir. That's built. Voir. Voir. Connected to view in English. Voir. To see. So how might you say I want to see her? Je veux la voir. Very good. Je veux la voir. How might you say I just want to see her? I want just to see her.
Je veux juste la voir. Very good. Je veux juste la voir. I want to see him later. I want to see him later.
Je veux le voir plus tard. Very good. Je veux le voir plus tard. Very good. Do you have to see him? Must you see him? Do you owe to see him?
Je dois. What's the first bit? You must, must you. Dois-tu le voir? Very good. Dois-tu or tu dois le voir? So voir ends differently to the verbs we've seen so far, which ends here. Voir ends here.

Voir. So voir ends I are and we hear the R here in voir. Voir. To see, like dois, must, like voiture, car has this OI combination giving us a what sound. The word for me is the same in French. Me. It's written the same but pronounced differently. It's written ME just like in English so how should that sound in French?

Me. Very good. With a weak E, like in G, like in Le. Me. Very good. And me, me, goes in the same position as Le, as La. It's the same type of word so it follows the same rules about where it should go. So how would you say do you want to see me? Do you want to see me? So the first bit is do you want? That's the only bit you should think about for now.
Vais-tu me voir? Good but not so much me but me. Good. Vais-tu me voir? Do you want to see me? Or just with the intonation only? Tu veux me voir? Can you see me? Are you able to see me?
Very good. Tu peux or peux-tu me voir? You must see me. You have to see me.
Must you provoke me? Must you provoke me?

Tu dois me provoquer? Tu dois. Dois tu me provoquer? Very good. So I used provoquer as another example of how we want to get in this happy two ways of analysing vocabulary and we found that we could have for example, revoquer from the same voquer root. We could have invoquer which is invoke in English.

So we noticed there how the i-n gave us an invoquer and this is because again the n on the end of the syllable is getting swallowed into the vowel just like what we saw with confirmé for example, comparé. The same thing is happening here. So we get an for our nasal i invoquer. So this will count for other i-n's that we find.
So like for example if we want to say invitation, how would that sound?
Invitation. Good. Invitation. Invitation. To invite then from invitation. Invite. Good. We take away the i-tion and then we add a e, our e-r ending. Invite. Very good. To invite. Can you invite him?

Petit invider. Very good. So this was very good. You know you thought there just at one bit at a time even though that forced you to rethink it a couple of times. Look how quickly you could do that. Thinking about just one thing at a time. Very good.
Very good. Peux-tu-tu-peux-l'inviter. Can you invite me? Peux-tu-m'inviter. Good. The same with the me here. We will blend the me. So we get m apostrophe inviter. Peux-tu-m'inviter. Very good.
